comment: Shared dialect-shaping conformance scenarios (2026-10-13).
The product has two implementations of the same manifest interpreter: the TypeScript reference
(packages/router-core/src/manifest-interpreter.ts and its siblings) and the Rust port
(apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/core/dialect_shaping.rs). Every scenario in this file is executed by
BOTH, so the shaping rules are pinned to each other by construction rather than by comments.
Drivers:
TypeScript: packages/router-core/test/dialect-conformance.test.ts
Rust:       apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/core/dialect_shaping.rs (a #[cfg(test)] module)
Scope: every shaping function, and it is now complete — `normalizeDialectMessages`,
`shapeToolDeclarations`, `shapeMessageContent`, `attachToolParts`, `readToolCalls`,
`textOfContent`, `blockField` and `translateFinishReason`. `attachToolParts` was the last one in
and waited longest, for a reason worth keeping: its output depends on *relations between
messages* (a tool result's name is resolved by looking back at the assistant turn that declared
the call, and a run of consecutive tool results collapses into one message), so its scenarios had
to be written from the semantics rather than from the signature — and both implementations agreed
with the authored expectations on the first run, which is the evidence that readings on both
sides were the same reading.
The two `shape*` kinds are the renderer seam: the TypeScript signatures take the template
renderer as an INJECTED callback (the interpreter owns rendering) while the Rust signatures
render internally. The reference driver therefore passes `renderTemplate` from `template.ts`
explicitly, and the Rust driver relies on `render_object`/`render_template`. Both template
engines are themselves a reference/port pair, so a divergence there could belong to either —
which is why the scenarios keep their templates to plain `{{placeholder}}` substitution and
nested objects, the part both engines implement identically by construction.
Comparison rule, applied identically by both drivers: parse the actual output as JSON, drop
every object key whose value is null (recursively), and compare to the expectation with the
same normalization applied. Rust serialises `Option::None` as an explicit null where TypeScript
omits an absent optional key; without the rule the two would disagree about absence, which is
not what these scenarios are testing.
Scenario kinds:
normalizeMessages — {messages, roleMap, systemField} -> {messages, systemContent}
shapeContent      — {messages, templates, contentField} -> [messages]
readToolCalls     — {blocks, shape} -> [{id?, name?, arguments?}]
textOfContent     — {content} -> string
blockField        — {block, path} -> value | null
finishReason      — {reason, map} -> string
shapeToolDeclarations — {tools, templates, wrapper?} -> tools
shapeMessageContent   — {messages, templates, contentField} -> [messages]
The last two are the renderer seam: the TypeScript signatures take the template renderer as an
INJECTED callback (the interpreter owns rendering) while the Rust signatures render internally.
The reference driver therefore passes `renderTemplate` from `template.ts` explicitly, and the
Rust driver relies on `render_object`/`render_template`. Both template engines are themselves a
reference/port pair, so a divergence here can be a divergence in either — which is why the
scenarios keep their templates to plain `{{placeholder}}` substitution and nested objects, the
part both engines implement identically by construction.

scenarios.name: roles: system is hoisted into systemField, tool becomes user, tool_call_id is dropped
roles: two system messages join with a blank line, and a role not in the map passes through verbatim
roles: with no systemField the hoisted content is dropped, never written where nothing reads it
roles: no map at all is a pass-through, so a manifest predating the field is unchanged
tool calls: the OpenAI shape, json-string arguments carried through as text
tool calls: the Gemini shape — no discriminator value, object arguments serialized on the way in
tool calls: a block matching the discriminator but carrying no name is not a call
text: a string, a null, and an unknown shape
text: an array of parts joins with single spaces, and an image becomes the placeholder
block field: a dotted path resolves through nested objects
block field: a path that is not there is absent, not an error
finish reason: a declared mapping wins
finish reason: an unmapped value passes through rather than becoming a default
finish reason: no map is a pass-through
tool declarations: each function renders through its own type's template, and an undeclared type passes through
tool declarations: a wrapper receives the rendered declarations under {{declarations}}
content: a text part renders through its template and the field is renamed to the dialect's own
content: an image part is offered both the bare bytes and a data URI
content: a part type with no template is left exactly as it was
tool parts: an assistant call becomes a content part and its result answers it
tool parts: consecutive results collapse into one message, and each resolves its own tool name by looking back
tool parts: a result whose content arrived as parts still carries its text
